narrative:
The model estimates a 70% probability that you will leave your job, meaning you are more likely than not to depart. Because of that high anticipated flight risk, the promotion is being denied: the organization sees a strong chance that any promotion investment may be lost if you leave.

The strongest signal was your total career experience in the 6–10 year range. Compared with employees predicted to stay, that range is less common than 1–5 years, and the model treated it as increasing your likelihood of leaving. Your 1–5 years in the current organization was the second strongest signal and also pushed toward leaving, even though it is the most common tenure among stayers. The main counterweight was that you reported no other job opportunities, which reduced the likelihood of leaving. Other context—low salary range, no deserved promotion so far, dissatisfaction with rewards, no job stability, difficult work–life balance, and physical stress—adds retention concern.

Before revisiting promotion, you should discuss career progression, pay and rewards, workload, stability, and development with your manager. The organization should treat this as a retention conversation, clarify promotion criteria, and consider targeted support such as compensation review, internal growth opportunities, and workload adjustments.
